title: Bereaved fathers and a Trojan response
intro: Diomedes’ victories are measured against the households they destroy. Dual forms again matter: several pairs of brothers die together. Aeneas finally seeks out Pandarus, whose archery reputation now becomes a challenge to act.

notes.text: σφεας is third-person accusative plural, ‘them.’ ἐξενάριξε is aorist of ἐξεναρίζω, ‘slay / strip of arms.’ βῆ is unaugmented root-aorist of βαίνω; μετά with accusative names the men he goes after. Φαίνοπος υἷε is accusative dual, ‘the two sons of Phaenops.’

τηλυγέτω is dual of τηλύγετος, conventionally ‘late-born / specially cherished’; the old father’s lack of another son makes that emotional force explicit. γήραϊ is uncontracted dative of γῆρας, ‘old age,’ with τείρετο, ‘was worn down.’ τέκετο is second-aorist middle of τίκτω, ‘begot.’ λιπέσθαι, from λείπω, expresses leaving another son to inherit.

κτέατα are possessions; κτεάτεσσι is epic dative plural. ἐξαίνυτο is imperfect middle of ἐξαίνυμαι, ‘took away,’ with θυμόν, life or vital spirit, as object. ἀμφοτέρω is accusative dual, referring to the brothers whose lives he removes. φίλος often marks what belongs intimately to someone: ‘their life,’ not ‘a friendly spirit.’

Both participles are accusative dual: ‘alive’ and ‘having returned from battle.’ They depend on δέξατο, ‘received,’ from δέχομαι, with the father as subject and a negative. γόος is lamentation; κήδεα are sorrows. χηρωσταί are collateral heirs who succeed when the direct line fails; διὰ … δατέοντο means they divided the estate among themselves.

The two genitives describe Priam, son or descendant of Dardanus. Δαρδανίδαο preserves the epic masculine genitive -αο. εἰν is an epic form of ἐν; ἑνί is dative of εἷς. ἐόντας is epic present participle of εἰμί: the two men are together in a single chariot.

θορών is second-aorist active participle of θρῴσκω, ‘leap.’ ἄξῃ is aorist subjunctive of ἄγνυμι, ‘break,’ not ἄγω; ἐξ supplies ‘break off.’ αὐχένα is the neck, and πόρτιος the genitive of πόρτις, ‘calf / heifer.’ The lion simile uses a generalized subjunctive. ξύλοχον κάτα has the preposition after its object, ‘through the thicket.’

βῆσε is the transitive sigmatic aorist of βαίνω, ‘made descend,’ contrasting with intransitive βῆ, ‘went.’ κακῶς ἀέκοντας conveys a forcible, disastrous dismounting. οἷς is possessive, ‘his own,’ agreeing with ἑτάροισι. δίδου is imperfect of δίδωμι; ἐλαύνειν gives the task assigned to the companions.

ἀλαπάζω means ‘empty, devastate, rout’; στίχας is accusative plural of στίξ, a row or battle line. βῆ ἴμεν combines a finite ‘went’ with epic infinitive ἴμεν from εἶμι, an idiomatic departure formula. ἄν is ἀνά here, not the modal particle; κλόνος is the turmoil of combat, and ἐγχειάων epic genitive plural of ἐγχείη, ‘spear.’

διζήμενος, from δίζημαι, means ‘seeking.’ εἴ που with optative ἐφεύροι conveys the tentative aim, ‘to see if he might find him somewhere.’ ἐφεύροι is aorist optative of ἐφευρίσκω. εὗρε then supplies the successful result. ἀντίον is adverbial with ηὔδα, ‘addressed him face to face.’

The question is a challenge to make good on his reputation, not simply a request to locate the bow. τοι is enclitic dative ‘your / for you.’ ᾧ refers to κλέος and gives the respect in which no rival contends with him. σέο is epic genitive ‘than you’ after comparative ἀμείνων; εὔχεται here means ‘claims.’

ἔφες is aorist active imperative of ἐφίημι, ‘send [an arrow] at’; τῷδε ἀνδρί is its target. ἀνασχών is second-aorist participle of ἀνέχω, ‘raising’ his hands to Zeus in prayer. ἔοργε is perfect active of ἔρδω, ‘has done.’ κακὰ … Τρῶας expresses doing harm to the Trojans; γούνατ᾽ ἔλυσε, ‘loosed the knees,’ is a recurring image of killing or disabling.
